newsitem.title: FRANCE: PSA Peugeot 1996 profit seen down sharply.
newsitem.headline: PSA Peugeot 1996 profit seen down sharply.

text.p: French carmaker PSA Peugeot Citroen SA is expected on Thursday morning to report a sharp fall in 1996 income, reflecting the damage caused by a price war in the French market, analysts said.

The brokers' consensus estimate compiled by Paris consultant Jacques Chahine Finance is for a net attributable profit of 1.2 billion francs ($206.7 million), compared with 1.70 billion for 1995, a 45 percent drop from the preceding year.
PSA Peugeot Citroen is expected to report its 1996 results at 0630 GMT and hold an analysts meeting later in the day.
The estimates span a wide range between 800 million francs and 1.7 billion, according to Jacques Chahine.

Although a second consecutive annual profit fall comes as a disappointment, particularly given the high level of sales volumes, the Peugeot group is faring much better than its domestic rival Renault SA.
Renault last month reported a 5.25 billion franc loss for 1996 after taking 3.9 billion francs in charges to close an assembly plant in Belgium and cut nearly 6,000 jobs in Europe.

"In the case of Peugeot, it is difficult not to have some sympathy," Goldman Sachs analyst Keith Hayes wrote in a report. "The company is, in our view, a victim of external events and not internal bad management."
With French car sales expected to fall around 10 percent this year and little growth expected for the rest of Europe, the group should also have a difficult time in 1997, he said.

Sales in 1996 were brisk due largely to a state rebate scheme that ran to the end of September 1996 and was matched by company discounts. Chairman Jacques Calvet said the two-tier rebate scheme did not skew demand as much as a prior flat-rate rebate programme but still encouraged sales of cheaper cars.

The group's revenues rose by 5.1 percent to 172.7 billion francs last year. "With volumes having risen 7.6 percent and with currency thought to have been neutral for the year as a whole, there appears to have been a negative impact caused in terms of mix and/or pricing. This was clear at Citroen, where volumes for the year rose by 12 percent whereas revenues only increased by three percent," Hayes said.

He said the sales figures revealed only part of the picture. The Peugeot group's accounting conventions mean part of the sales incentives are recorded as 'other external costs', an item that has jumped to an estimated 15.7 percent of revenues from nine percent in 1987.

Analyst Sabine Bluemel at IMI Sigeco is looking for a profit of 1.1 billion francs, or 21 francs per share, slightly under the consensus. "We therefore anticipate PSA to cut its dividend again, to four francs per share," she wrote in a note.

"People will be watching to see what they have to say about the first quarter of 1997," said another analyst. New car sales in France were down 26.5 percent in the first three months of the year from inflated 1996 first-quarter levels.
Major cost-cutting programmes similar to those undertaken at Renault are not expected as Chairman Jacques Calvet is expected to retire in the autumn.

Under company bylaws, the chairman must retire within a year of his 65th birthday. Calvet turned 65 in September. The company has not announced a successor but he is widely believed to be Jean-Martin Folz, who came to PSA in January 1996, leaving a job as managing director of food giant Eridania Beghin-Say.
-- Christine Tierney, Paris Newsroom, +33 1 4221 5452 ($ = 5.804 French Francs)
